title: The Gita in 18 Days
intro: One verse from each of the Bhagavad Gita's 18 chapters, ending on Gita Jayanti.

posts.caption: Gita Jayanti, the day traditionally marking when Krishna spoke the Gita, falls on December 20 this year for many. Until then, one verse from each of its 18 chapters. Chapter 1, Arjuna Vishada Yoga, ends here: overwhelmed at the thought of fighting his own family, Arjuna puts down his bow.

Chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, holds Krishna's first great teaching: the self that is never born and never dies, and how to act without clinging to results. This verse joins the two. Samatva, evenness of mind in success and failure, is here called yoga itself.

Chapter 3, Karma Yoga, argues that no one can stop acting even for a moment, so the real question is how to act. Krishna's answer: with the senses guided by the mind, and without attachment to results. Besant's "yoga by action" is karma yoga itself. Done this way, action becomes yajna, an offering, rather than a bond.

Chapter 4 traces this teaching back to the sun god Vivasvan and ancient kings, tells of Krishna's own births, and joins action to knowledge. This verse gathers its threads: someone who has let go of action through yoga, acting without clinging, and has cut away doubt with wisdom is no longer bound by anything they do. Its traditional title, Jnana Karma Sannyasa Yoga, names knowledge, action and renunciation.

Chapter 5 takes up Arjuna's question: renounce action, or act in the spirit of yoga? Krishna says both reach one goal, and toward the chapter's end describes it: brahma-nirvana, the peace of the Eternal, close at hand for those free of desire and krodha, anger (Besant's "passion"). Shankara favours renunciation for the knower; Tilak and Gandhi stress engaged action.

Chapter 6, Dhyana Yoga, is the Gita's chapter on meditation: a quiet place, a steady seat, moderation in food and sleep, and a one-pointed mind. Arjuna protests that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna agrees, and says it can be trained through practice and detachment.

Chapter 7 is about knowing God fully. Krishna describes himself as present in everything, the taste in water and the light of sun and moon, yet hidden from most by yogamaya, his own veiling power, which Besant calls "creation-illusion." The chapter ends by describing those who do come to know him.

Chapter 8 asks what happens at death and what lies beyond the great cycles of the cosmos. Even the highest worlds, up to that of Brahma the creator, come and go in endless return. For one who reaches Krishna, the chapter says, rebirth comes to an end.

Chapter 9 is called Raja Vidya Raja Guhya Yoga, the yoga of the royal knowledge and the royal secret, which Krishna begins to reveal here. The secret is how near he is: present in all things, and accepting even the simplest offering of a leaf or a flower given with love.

Chapter 10, Vibhuti Yoga, lists Krishna's vibhutis, his divine glories in the world: among rivers the Ganga, among the immovable the Himalaya, among letters the first, A. Near the end he says the list could go on forever; what he has named is only a sample.

In chapter 11, Arjuna, the Pandava or "son of Pandu," asks to see Krishna's universal form and is given divine sight to see it: the whole universe in one body, blazing like a thousand suns. Awestruck and afraid, he finally asks Krishna to return to his familiar form. The chapter is called Vishvarupa Darshana Yoga, the vision of the universal form.

Chapter 12, Bhakti Yoga, is one of the Gita's two shortest chapters, at 20 verses. Arjuna asks who is better: those who worship Krishna in personal form, or those who meditate on the formless. Krishna's answer: those who fix their minds on him with constant devotion and supreme faith are the most perfect in yoga. Those who seek the formless reach him too, he adds, but by a path harder for embodied beings.

Chapter 13 distinguishes the kshetra, the "field" of body and matter, from the kshetrajna, the "knower of the field," the conscious self. This verse names true vision: seeing the same Lord dwelling equally in all beings. Whoever sees this way, Krishna says, does not harm the Self, which commentators take to mean no longer mistaking oneself for the body, and so reaches the highest goal. Many editions number this verse 13:28.

Chapter 14 explains the three gunas, the qualities of nature that bind the self to the body: sattva (clarity), rajas (activity) and tamas (inertia), Besant's Harmony, Motion and Inertia. Its answer to how one rises beyond all three is unwavering devotion.

Chapter 15 opens with the world pictured as an ashvattha, a sacred fig tree, with roots above and branches below. It closes by naming Krishna Purushottama, the supreme person, beyond both the perishable and the imperishable. Whoever truly knows him so, this verse says, knows all there is to know and worships him with their whole being: here knowledge and devotion meet. The chapter is called Purushottama Yoga.

Chapter 16 contrasts two kinds of nature: the divine (daivi), with qualities like fearlessness, compassion and truthfulness, and the demonic (asuri), pictured here as driven by insatiable desire, vanity and arrogance. Krishna assures Arjuna that he is born with the divine qualities, and names desire, anger and greed as the gates to ruin.

Chapter 17 is about shraddha, faith. Faith takes three forms according to the gunas, and the chapter traces them through worship, food, austerity and giving. It ends with Aum Tat Sat, three words naming the ultimate reality. Gita Jayanti falls tomorrow for many.

Gita Jayanti falls today for many, on Mokshada Ekadashi, the day tradition marks as when Krishna spoke the Gita. Chapter 18 gathers the whole teaching; Arjuna's doubts are gone, and he is ready to act. Sanjaya, narrating to the blind king, ends in wonder at what he has heard. Thank you for reading the Gita in 18 days.
